etymology: Hebrew Mikha'el (who is like God?). The archangel named in Daniel (10:13, 21; 12:1), Jude (1:9), and Revelation (12:7). The only angel explicitly called archangel in Scripture (Jude 1:9); the prince who stands for God's people and contends against the dragon.
biblical_def: Hebrew Mikha'el (who is like God?), the archangel named in the canonical Scriptures. Michael appears in five passages. (1) Daniel 10:13, where he is called one of the chief princes who came to help the angelic messenger withstand the prince of Persia (a demonic principality). (2) Daniel 10:21, Michael your prince, the angelic guardian of God's people. (3) Daniel 12:1, Michael shall stand up, the great prince which standeth for the children of thy people, associated with the time of the end and the deliverance of God's people. (4) Jude 1:9, where Michael the archangel, when contending with the devil he disputed about the body of Moses, durst not bring against him a railing accusation, but said, The Lord rebuke thee — the only place in Scripture where the title archangel (chief angel) is explicitly applied to a named angel, and a model of the angelic refusal to usurp God's prerogative of judgment. (5) Revelation 12:7, there was war in heaven: Michael and his angels fought against the dragon; and the dragon fought and his angels, where Michael leads the heavenly host against Satan. Michael is the warrior-prince of the angelic host, the guardian of God's covenant people, and the leader of the heavenly armies against the dragon. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive biblical doctrine of Michael against both the neglect of angelology (which ignores the reality of the angelic host) and the speculative excess (the elaborate angel-hierarchies and angel-veneration of medieval Catholicism and contemporary new-age angelology). Michael is a created angel, however exalted, not to be worshiped (Revelation 22:8-9, the angel refuses worship); his very name (who is like God?) is a rhetorical confession of God's incomparable supremacy.

corruption_paragraphs: Michael as a proper name does not undergo lexical corruption. The two principal mishandlings of the doctrine of Michael are opposite. The medieval-Catholic and contemporary new-age tendency exalts Michael into an object of veneration, prayer, and devotion (the cult of St. Michael; the new-age angel-channeling and angel-devotion movements); this contradicts the explicit biblical refusal of angel-worship (Revelation 22:8-9; Colossians 2:18, the warning against the worshipping of angels). The rationalist neglect dismisses or ignores the biblical doctrine of the angelic host altogether, treating Michael and the angels as mythological. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive biblical doctrine: Michael is a real created angel, exalted as the archangel and warrior-prince of the heavenly host, the guardian of God's covenant people and the leader of the heavenly armies against the dragon — but a creature, not to be worshiped, whose very name confesses God's incomparable supremacy (who is like God?).

etymology: Hebrew Gavri'el (man of God or God is my strength). The angelic messenger named in Daniel (8:16; 9:21) and Luke (1:19, 26). The herald-angel who interprets visions and announces the births of John the Baptist and the Lord Jesus.
biblical_def: Hebrew Gavri'el (man of God or God is my strength), the angelic messenger named in four canonical passages. (1) Daniel 8:16, where Gabriel is commanded to make Daniel understand the vision of the ram and the goat. (2) Daniel 9:21-23, where Gabriel comes to Daniel at the time of the evening sacrifice to give him understanding of the prophecy of the seventy weeks. (3) Luke 1:19, where Gabriel announces to Zacharias the coming birth of John the Baptist, identifying himself: I am Gabriel, that stand in the presence of God; and am sent to speak unto thee, and to shew thee these glad tidings. (4) Luke 1:26-38, where Gabriel is sent to the virgin Mary in Nazareth to announce the conception and birth of the Lord Jesus (the Annunciation), declaring Hail, thou that art highly favoured, the Lord is with thee... thou shalt conceive in thy womb, and bring forth a son, and shalt call his name JESUS. Gabriel is the herald-angel, the interpreter of visions and the announcer of the two most consequential births in redemptive history (the forerunner and the Messiah). He stands in the presence of God (Luke 1:19), among the highest of the angelic host. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive biblical doctrine of Gabriel: a real created angel, the messenger and herald of God, the interpreter of prophetic visions and the announcer of the births of John and Jesus — a creature in the service of God's redemptive purposes, not an object of worship or devotion.

The Catholic and new-age tendency exalts Gabriel into an object of veneration and devotion; this contradicts the biblical refusal of angel-worship (Revelation 22:8-9). etymology: The doctrine that God assigns angels to watch over and minister to His people. Grounded in Hebrews 1:14 (angels as ministering spirits, sent forth to minister for them who shall be heirs of salvation), Psalm 91:11 (he shall give his angels charge over thee), and Matthew 18:10 (the children's angels who behold the Father's face).
biblical_def: The doctrine that God assigns angels to watch over, protect, and minister to His people. The biblical foundation is substantial, though the precise scope (whether each believer has an individual personal guardian angel) is debated. The key texts: (1) Hebrews 1:14, the general ministry of angels to the heirs of salvation, Are they not all ministering spirits, sent forth to minister for them who shall be heirs of salvation?; (2) Psalm 91:11-12, For he shall give his angels charge over thee, to keep thee in all thy ways. They shall bear thee up in their hands, lest thou dash thy foot against a stone (cited by Satan in the temptation of Christ, Matthew 4:6); (3) Matthew 18:10, the Lord Jesus's words concerning the little ones, that in heaven their angels do always behold the face of my Father which is in heaven, which has been understood by many as supporting individual guardian angels; (4) Acts 12:15, where the believers gathered in prayer, hearing that Peter was at the door, said it is his angel, reflecting an early-Christian belief in personal guardian angels; (5) Psalm 34:7, The angel of the LORD encampeth round about them that fear him, and delivereth them; (6) 2 Kings 6:17, the angelic host surrounding Elisha at Dothan. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive biblical doctrine: God ministers to and protects His people through the agency of angels; the angelic host is real and active in the providential care of the saints. The Reformed tradition affirms the ministry of angels while exercising caution about the more speculative elaborations (the precise assignment of individual personal guardian angels to each believer is held by some and regarded as uncertain by others; the doctrine should not become a substitute for direct dependence on God Himself, nor an occasion for angel-veneration). The substantive comfort of the doctrine is that the believer is surrounded and ministered to by the unseen angelic host in the providential care of his heavenly Father.

etymology: The doctrine that a portion of the angels rebelled against God and fell from their original holy estate, becoming the demons. Grounded in 2 Peter 2:4 (the angels that sinned), Jude 1:6 (the angels which kept not their first estate), and Revelation 12:4, 9 (the dragon drawing the third part of the stars / casting down with his angels).
biblical_def: The doctrine that a portion of the angels rebelled against God, fell from their original holy estate, and became the demons (the evil spirits in the service of Satan). The biblical foundation: (1) 2 Peter 2:4, God spared not the angels that sinned, but cast them down to hell, and delivered them into chains of darkness, to be reserved unto judgment; (2) Jude 1:6, the angels which kept not their first estate, but left their own habitation, he hath reserved in everlasting chains under darkness unto the judgment of the great day; (3) Revelation 12:4, 9, where the dragon's tail draws the third part of the stars of heaven and casts them to the earth, and the dragon is cast out with his angels (commonly understood to depict the fall of Satan and the angels who followed him); (4) John 8:44, where the devil is described as a murderer and liar from the beginning, abiding not in the truth; (5) 1 John 3:8, the devil sinneth from the beginning. The doctrine holds that the angels were created holy; that some (led by Satan) rebelled against God in a pre-temporal or primeval fall; that these fallen angels became the demons, irredeemably confirmed in their rebellion (unlike fallen humanity, there is no redemption offered to the fallen angels, Hebrews 2:16, he took not on him the nature of angels; but he took on him the seed of Abraham); and that they are reserved in chains of darkness unto the judgment of the great day. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive biblical doctrine: the fallen angels are real, the demons are the fallen angels in the service of Satan, their rebellion is irredeemable, and their final judgment is certain (Matthew 25:41, the everlasting fire prepared for the devil and his angels). The doctrine is held against the rationalist denial of the spirit-realm and against the speculative excess (the elaborate fallen-angel mythologies of apocryphal and new-age literature).

webster_full: FALLEN ANGELS, n. phr. (angelology / demonology) A portion of the angels rebelled against God, fell from their original holy estate, and became the demons. Foundation: 2 Peter 2:4 (the angels that sinned... cast down to hell... reserved unto judgment); Jude 1:6 (the angels which kept not their first estate); Revelation 12:4, 9 (the dragon and his angels cast down); John 8:44; 1 John 3:8. The angels were created holy; some (led by Satan) rebelled in a primeval fall; the fallen angels became the demons, irredeemably confirmed in rebellion (no redemption offered, Hebrews 2:16); reserved in chains of darkness unto the judgment of the great day; their final judgment certain (Matthew 25:41, the everlasting fire prepared for the devil and his angels).

corruption_summary: The fallen angels are real, irredeemable, and certainly to be judged; the corruptions are the rationalist denial of the spirit-realm and the speculative fallen-angel mythologies of apocryphal and new-age literature.
corruption_paragraphs: Fallen angels as a doctrine is held against two opposing errors. The rationalist denial dismisses the spirit-realm altogether, treating Satan and the demons as mythological symbols of evil rather than real personal spiritual beings; this contradicts the substantive biblical witness to the reality of the fallen angels (2 Peter 2:4; Jude 1:6; the Lord Jesus's own confrontations with demons throughout the Gospels). The speculative excess elaborates the fall of the angels into detailed mythologies drawn from apocryphal literature (1 Enoch, the elaborate watcher-Nephilim narratives) and new-age angelology, going far beyond the substantive biblical data. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive biblical doctrine within its proper bounds: the angels were created holy; some rebelled (led by Satan) and fell from their first estate; the fallen angels became the demons in the service of Satan; their rebellion is irredeemable (Christ took on the seed of Abraham, not the nature of angels, to redeem fallen humanity but not fallen angels, Hebrews 2:16); they are reserved in chains of darkness unto judgment; and their final judgment in the everlasting fire is certain (Matthew 25:41). The doctrine sobers the believer to the reality of the spiritual conflict (Ephesians 6:12) while assuring him of the certain final defeat and judgment of the fallen angelic host.

etymology: Hebrew satan (adversary, accuser); Greek satanas. The personal name and title of the chief of the fallen angels, the adversary of God and His people, also called the devil (diabolos, slanderer), the serpent, the dragon, the prince of this world, the god of this age, and the prince of the power of the air.
biblical_def: Hebrew satan (adversary, accuser); the personal name and title of the chief of the fallen angels, the great adversary of God and His people. Scripture reveals Satan under many names and titles: the devil (Greek diabolos, slanderer, accuser; Matthew 4:1); that old serpent (Revelation 12:9, 20:2, recalling Genesis 3); the great dragon (Revelation 12:9); the prince of this world (John 12:31; 14:30; 16:11); the god of this world / age (2 Corinthians 4:4); the prince of the power of the air (Ephesians 2:2); Beelzebub, the prince of the devils (Matthew 12:24); the accuser of our brethren (Revelation 12:10); Apollyon / Abaddon (the destroyer, Revelation 9:11); the tempter (Matthew 4:3); the wicked one (Matthew 13:19, 38). The biblical doctrine of Satan: he is a real personal being, a fallen angel (the chief of the fallen angels); he fell from his original holy estate through pride and rebellion; he is the adversary who tempts (Genesis 3; Matthew 4; the temptation of Christ), accuses (Job 1-2; Zechariah 3:1; Revelation 12:10), deceives (Revelation 12:9, which deceiveth the whole world; 2 Corinthians 11:14, transforming himself into an angel of light), and seeks to devour (1 Peter 5:8, your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour); he is a creature, not a rival deity (the dualistic error), under God's sovereign control (Job 1-2, Satan can act only within the bounds God permits); he was decisively defeated at the cross and resurrection (Hebrews 2:14; Colossians 2:15; 1 John 3:8); he is destined for final judgment in the lake of fire (Revelation 20:10). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive biblical doctrine of Satan against both the rationalist denial (Satan as a mythological symbol of evil) and the dualistic exaltation (Satan as a near-equal rival to God). Satan is a real, personal, powerful, but created and defeated adversary, under the sovereign control of God and destined for certain judgment.

webster_full: SATAN, proper n. (demonology; Hebrew satan, adversary, accuser; Greek satanas) The chief of the fallen angels, the great adversary of God and His people. Many names: the devil (slanderer); that old serpent and great dragon (Revelation 12:9); the prince of this world (John 12:31); the god of this age (2 Corinthians 4:4); the prince of the power of the air (Ephesians 2:2); the accuser of the brethren (Revelation 12:10); the tempter (Matthew 4:3). A real personal fallen angel; fell through pride and rebellion; tempts (Genesis 3; Matthew 4), accuses (Job 1-2; Revelation 12:10), deceives (2 Corinthians 11:14), seeks to devour (1 Peter 5:8). A creature under God's sovereign control (Job 1-2), not a rival deity; decisively defeated at the cross (Hebrews 2:14; Colossians 2:15); destined for the lake of fire (Revelation 20:10).

corruption_summary: Satan is a real, personal, created, and defeated adversary under God's sovereign control; the corruptions are the rationalist denial (Satan as a symbol of evil) and the dualistic exaltation (Satan as a near-equal rival to God).
corruption_paragraphs: Satan as a doctrine is held against two opposing errors. The rationalist denial treats Satan as a mythological symbol of evil rather than a real personal being; this contradicts the substantive biblical witness (the Lord Jesus's personal confrontations with Satan in the temptation, Matthew 4; the consistent biblical presentation of Satan as a personal adversary who tempts, accuses, and deceives). The dualistic exaltation treats Satan as a near-equal rival to God, a co-eternal principle of evil locked in cosmic struggle with the principle of good (the Manichaean and Zoroastrian dualisms, and various popular semi-dualistic conceptions); this contradicts the biblical doctrine that Satan is a creature, a fallen angel, under God's sovereign control (Job 1-2, where Satan can act only within the bounds God permits), decisively defeated at the cross (Colossians 2:15), and destined for certain judgment (Revelation 20:10). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive biblical doctrine: Satan is real, personal, powerful, and active — the believer must be sober and vigilant (1 Peter 5:8), resist him (James 4:7), and stand against his wiles (Ephesians 6:11) — but he is a creature, not a rival deity; under God's sovereign control; decisively defeated at the cross; and destined for the lake of fire. The believer's confidence is in the certain victory of Christ over Satan, not in fear of an exalted devil.

etymology: Greek daimonion (evil spirit, demon). The fallen angels in the service of Satan; the evil spirits that oppose God, afflict and possess men, and promote idolatry and deception. Distinguished in Scripture from the holy angels by their rebellion and corruption.
biblical_def: Greek daimonion (evil spirit, demon); the fallen angels in the service of Satan, the evil spirits that oppose God, afflict and possess men, and promote idolatry and deception. The biblical doctrine of demons. (1) Their identity: demons are the fallen angels (the angels that sinned, 2 Peter 2:4; Jude 1:6; Satan's angels, Matthew 25:41; Revelation 12:9), real personal spiritual beings in rebellion against God. (2) Their activity: demons tempt to sin; afflict with physical and mental torment (the demoniacs of the Gospels); possess men (Mark 5:1-20, the Gerasene demoniac; many Gospel accounts); promote idolatry (1 Corinthians 10:20, the things which the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to devils, and not to God); spread false doctrine (1 Timothy 4:1, doctrines of devils); and oppose the kingdom of God. (3) Their subjection to Christ: the demons recognize and fear Christ (Mark 1:24, I know thee who thou art, the Holy One of God; James 2:19, the devils also believe, and tremble); they are cast out by Christ's authority and the authority He gave His disciples (Matthew 10:1; Luke 10:17-20; Acts 16:18); they are wholly subject to His sovereign power. (4) Their destiny: the demons face certain final judgment (Matthew 25:41, the everlasting fire prepared for the devil and his angels). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive biblical doctrine of demons against both the rationalist denial (demons as primitive explanations for disease and mental illness) and the demon-obsessed excess (the hyper-charismatic demon-behind-every-bush spirituality, the elaborate deliverance-ministry systems, the territorial-spirits and generational-curses schemes). Demons are real, personal, fallen-angelic beings, active in opposition to God and His people, but wholly subject to the sovereign authority of Christ; the believer resists them through the means God has appointed (the armor of God, Ephesians 6; sober vigilance, 1 Peter 5:8; submission to God and resistance of the devil, James 4:7) and rests in the certain victory of Christ over the whole demonic host.
webster_summary: Greek daimonion; the fallen angels in the service of Satan; evil spirits that tempt, afflict, possess, and promote idolatry and false doctrine; real personal beings wholly subject to the authority of Christ; destined for certain judgment (Matthew 25:41).
webster_full: DEMONS (DOCTRINE), n. (demonology; Greek daimonion, evil spirit) The fallen angels in the service of Satan; the evil spirits opposing God. Identity: the fallen angels (2 Peter 2:4; Matthew 25:41; Revelation 12:9). Activity: tempt to sin; afflict and possess (the Gospel demoniacs, Mark 5:1-20); promote idolatry (1 Corinthians 10:20); spread false doctrine (1 Timothy 4:1). Subjection to Christ: recognize and fear Him (Mark 1:24; James 2:19, the devils also believe, and tremble); cast out by His authority (Matthew 10:1; Luke 10:17-20). Destiny: certain final judgment (Matthew 25:41). Held against the rationalist denial and the demon-obsessed hyper-charismatic excess; demons are real but wholly subject to Christ's sovereign authority.

corruption_paragraphs: Demons as a doctrine is held against two opposing errors. etymology: The question of rank and order among the angels. Scripture refers to various angelic ranks and types (cherubim, seraphim, archangels, thrones, dominions, principalities, powers) without providing a complete systematic hierarchy; the elaborate nine-order hierarchy of Pseudo-Dionysius is a later speculative systematization the Reformed tradition treats with caution.
biblical_def: The question of rank and order among the angels. Scripture indicates that the angels are not an undifferentiated mass but are ordered in ranks and types, while not providing a complete systematic hierarchy. The biblical data: (1) Cherubim, the angelic guardians associated with God's holiness and throne (Genesis 3:24; Exodus 25:18-22, the cherubim over the mercy seat; Ezekiel 1, 10; the living creatures); (2) Seraphim, the burning ones who attend God's throne crying holy, holy, holy (Isaiah 6:2-3); (3) Archangels, the chief angels (Michael, Jude 1:9; the archangel's voice, 1 Thessalonians 4:16); (4) the Pauline references to angelic ranks among the principalities and powers: thrones, dominions, principalities, powers (Colossians 1:16; also Ephesians 1:21, principality, and power, and might, and dominion; Ephesians 3:10; 6:12; Romans 8:38); (5) the chief princes (Daniel 10:13, Michael one of the chief princes); (6) the innumerable angelic host (Daniel 7:10, thousand thousands ministered unto him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him; Hebrews 12:22, an innumerable company of angels; Revelation 5:11). The biblical data thus indicates ranks and types of angels (cherubim, seraphim, archangels, and the various principalities and powers) without providing a complete systematic hierarchy. The elaborate nine-order angelic hierarchy of Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite (The Celestial Hierarchy, c. 5th-6th century, arranging the angels in three triads of three orders each: seraphim, cherubim, thrones; dominions, virtues, powers; principalities, archangels, angels) was enormously influential in medieval Catholic theology (Thomas Aquinas, Dante's Paradiso) but is a speculative systematization that goes beyond the biblical data. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive biblical data (the angels are ordered in ranks and types) while treating the elaborate Pseudo-Dionysian hierarchy with appropriate caution as speculative beyond Scripture. The substantive point is that the angelic host is real, vast, ordered, and arrayed in the service of God's glory and the ministry of His people, without an exhaustive systematic hierarchy revealed in Scripture.

etymology: The condition in which a demon or demons inhabit and control a person, attested extensively in the Gospels (the demoniacs whom Christ delivered). Greek daimonizomai (to be demon-possessed, demonized). Distinguished from ordinary sin, illness, and mental disorder, though the Gospels also distinguish demonic affliction from natural illness.
biblical_def: The condition in which a demon or demons inhabit and control a person, attested extensively in the Gospels. The Greek verb daimonizomai (to be demon-possessed, demonized) and related expressions describe a range of demonic affliction. The Gospel accounts: the Gerasene/Gadarene demoniac possessed by a legion of demons (Mark 5:1-20; Matthew 8:28-34; Luke 8:26-39); the demon-possessed boy with seizure-like symptoms (Mark 9:14-29); the Syrophoenician woman's demon-possessed daughter (Mark 7:24-30); the demoniac in the Capernaum synagogue (Mark 1:23-28); the mute demoniac (Matthew 9:32-33); the blind and mute demoniac (Matthew 12:22); Mary Magdalene out of whom went seven demons (Luke 8:2). The biblical phenomena of demonic possession include: the demon speaking through the possessed person (Mark 1:24; 5:7-9); supernatural strength (Mark 5:3-4); self-destructive behavior (Mark 5:5; 9:22); recognition of Christ's identity and authority (Mark 1:24; 5:7); and torment relieved at Christ's command. The Gospels carefully distinguish demonic affliction from ordinary illness (Matthew 4:24, those which were possessed with devils, and those which were lunatick, and those that had the palsy are listed distinctly), indicating that the biblical authors did not simply attribute all disease to demons. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive biblical doctrine of demonic possession against both the rationalist denial (which dismisses possession as a pre-scientific explanation for epilepsy and mental illness) and the demon-obsessed excess (which attributes nearly every difficulty to demonic possession requiring elaborate deliverance ministry). Demonic possession is real, attested in Scripture, and a manifestation of the demonic host's opposition to God and affliction of men; it is overcome by the sovereign authority of Christ; the believer who is indwelt by the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:19; Romans 8:9) is held by the Reformed tradition not to be subject to demonic possession in the full sense, though Christians may be afflicted, tempted, and oppressed by demonic activity. The substantive remedy is the authority of Christ, exercised through the appointed means of grace, prayer, and (in the apostolic era) the direct casting out of demons by Christ's authority.

etymology: The casting out of demons by divine authority. Greek ekballo ta daimonia (to cast out demons). Practiced by the Lord Jesus throughout the Gospels and by the disciples He commissioned; distinguished from the pagan incantation-exorcism and from later elaborate ritual-exorcism systems.
biblical_def: The casting out of demons by divine authority. The Greek phrase is ekballo ta daimonia (to cast out the demons); the Lord Jesus practiced exorcism throughout His ministry, and He commissioned His disciples to do the same. The biblical pattern: (1) Christ cast out demons by His own divine authority, with a word, not by incantation or ritual (Mark 1:25, Hold thy peace, and come out of him; Matthew 8:16, he cast out the spirits with his word); the demons recognized His authority and obeyed (Mark 1:27). (2) Christ's exorcisms were a sign of the inbreaking kingdom (Matthew 12:28, if I cast out devils by the Spirit of God, then the kingdom of God is come unto you); the binding of the strong man (Matthew 12:29). (3) Christ commissioned His disciples to cast out demons in His name (Matthew 10:1, 8; Mark 6:7, 13; Luke 9:1; 10:17, even the devils are subject unto us through thy name); the apostolic exorcisms in Acts (Acts 16:18, Paul casting out the spirit of divination; Acts 19:11-12). (4) Exorcism by Christ's name requires genuine relationship to Christ, not mere formula: the sons of Sceva who attempted to cast out demons by invoking Jesus whom Paul preacheth without genuine faith were overpowered by the demon (Acts 19:13-16); and Christ warns that some who cast out demons in His name will be rejected if they are workers of iniquity (Matthew 7:22-23). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive biblical doctrine of exorcism with appropriate discernment. The casting out of demons was a prominent feature of Christ's earthly ministry and the apostolic era, a sign of the inbreaking kingdom and the defeat of Satan's domain. The Reformed tradition is generally cautious about the contemporary practice of formal exorcism / deliverance ministry, distinguishing the substantive biblical reality (the authority of Christ over the demonic host) from the elaborate ritual-exorcism systems (the Catholic rite of exorcism, the hyper-charismatic deliverance-ministry industry) that often go beyond the biblical pattern. The substantive remedy for demonic affliction in the believer's life is the authority and sufficiency of Christ, exercised through the ordinary means of grace, prayer, the armor of God, and submission to God with resistance of the devil (James 4:7) — resting in the sovereign victory of Christ rather than in elaborate exorcism techniques.

corruption_paragraphs: Exorcism as a doctrine is held with substantive biblical warrant but appropriate Reformed discernment. The pagan corruption treats exorcism as a matter of incantation, formula, and ritual technique, attempting to manipulate the spirit-world by the right words; the sons of Sceva exemplify this corruption, attempting to cast out demons by invoking Jesus whom Paul preacheth as a magic formula without genuine faith, and being overpowered (Acts 19:13-16). The Catholic rite of exorcism and the hyper-charismatic deliverance-ministry industry, while not identical to pagan incantation, often develop elaborate ritual-and-technique systems that go beyond the substantive biblical pattern (Christ cast out demons with a word, by His own authority, not by elaborate ritual). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive biblical doctrine within its proper bounds: the casting out of demons was a prominent feature of Christ's earthly ministry and the apostolic era, a sign of the inbreaking kingdom and the defeat of Satan's domain, accomplished by the sovereign authority of Christ. The contemporary believer's confidence in the face of demonic affliction rests in the authority and sufficiency of Christ, exercised through the ordinary means of grace, prayer, the armor of God (Ephesians 6:10-18), and submission to God with resistance of the devil (James 4:7) — not in elaborate exorcism techniques, which can themselves become a fear-driven displacement of the believer's confidence in the finished victory of Christ (Colossians 2:15).

etymology: The doctrine of Satan's original fall from his holy estate through pride and rebellion. The name Lucifer (Latin light-bearer, from the Vulgate rendering of Hebrew helel, day star / shining one, Isaiah 14:12) became the traditional name for the pre-fall Satan. The classic prooftexts (Isaiah 14:12-15; Ezekiel 28:12-19) are debated as to their precise reference.
biblical_def: The doctrine of Satan's original fall from his holy estate through pride and rebellion against God. The name Lucifer (Latin lux + ferre, light-bearer) derives from the Vulgate's rendering of the Hebrew helel ben-shachar (day star, son of the morning / shining one) in Isaiah 14:12, and became the traditional name for the pre-fall Satan. The classic prooftexts and their interpretive debate: (1) Isaiah 14:12-15, How art thou fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, son of the morning!... For thou hast said in thine heart, I will ascend into heaven, I will exalt my throne above the stars of God... I will be like the most High. Yet thou shalt be brought down to hell; the immediate context is a taunt against the king of Babylon (Isaiah 14:4), but the language has traditionally been understood (by many of the Fathers and the Reformers) as also describing, by extension or typologically, the fall of Satan through pride. (2) Ezekiel 28:12-19, the lament over the king of Tyre, describing one who was perfect in beauty... in Eden the garden of God... the anointed cherub... perfect in thy ways from the day that thou wast created, till iniquity was found in thee... thine heart was lifted up because of thy beauty; again the immediate context is the king of Tyre, but the language (the cherub in Eden, perfect till iniquity was found) has traditionally been understood as describing, by extension, the fall of Satan. The substantive doctrine, whether or not these specific texts directly describe Satan's fall, is established by the broader biblical witness: Satan was created holy (as all the angels were, the original very-good creation, Genesis 1:31); he fell through pride and rebellion (1 Timothy 3:6 warns against the novice elder being lifted up with pride and falling into the condemnation of the devil, indicating pride as the cause of the devil's fall); he became the adversary, the chief of the fallen angels. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive doctrine of Satan's fall through pride with appropriate exegetical care regarding the Isaiah 14 and Ezekiel 28 prooftexts (acknowledging the immediate human-king referents while recognizing the traditional extended application to Satan), and notes the substantive moral lesson: pride was the cause of the devil's fall, and pride remains the great peril (the warning of 1 Timothy 3:6; Proverbs 16:18, pride goeth before destruction).

corruption_paragraphs: The fall of Lucifer as a doctrine requires appropriate exegetical care. The two classic prooftexts (Isaiah 14:12-15 and Ezekiel 28:12-19) have immediate referents that are human kings — the king of Babylon (Isaiah 14:4) and the king of Tyre (Ezekiel 28:12) — and some modern interpreters hold that these texts refer only to the human kings, not to Satan. The traditional interpretation (held by many of the Fathers and the Reformers) recognizes the immediate human-king referents while understanding the language (the fall from heaven, the ascent above the stars of God, the anointed cherub in Eden, the perfection till iniquity was found) as also describing, by extension or typologically, the fall of Satan through pride. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive doctrine with this exegetical care: whether or not these specific texts directly describe Satan's fall, the broader biblical witness establishes that Satan was created holy, fell through pride and rebellion, and became the chief of the fallen angels (1 Timothy 3:6 explicitly attributes the devil's condemnation to pride; Luke 10:18, the Lord Jesus beholding Satan fall as lightning from heaven). The substantive moral lesson is sobering and central: pride was the cause of the devil's fall, and pride remains the great peril for men and especially for those in spiritual office (1 Timothy 3:6; Proverbs 16:18, pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall). The doctrine warns the believer against the pride that destroyed the highest of the angels.

etymology: The divine attribute by which God is without beginning or end, transcending time, existing in the fullness of His being in an eternal present. Grounded in the divine names and self-descriptions (Psalm 90:2, from everlasting to everlasting, thou art God; Exodus 3:14, I AM THAT I AM; Revelation 1:8, which is, and which was, and which is to come).
biblical_def: The divine attribute by which God is without beginning or end, transcending time, existing in the fullness of His being in an eternal present. God's eternality means more than mere endless duration (existing through infinite time); it means that God transcends time itself, existing in the fullness of His being independent of and above the temporal succession of moments. The biblical foundation: (1) Psalm 90:2, Before the mountains were brought forth, or ever thou hadst formed the earth and the world, even from everlasting to everlasting, thou art God; (2) Exodus 3:14, the divine name I AM THAT I AM (the untensed, pure being of God); (3) Revelation 1:8, I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the ending, saith the Lord, which is, and which was, and which is to come, the Almighty; (4) Psalm 102:27, thou art the same, and thy years shall have no end; (5) 2 Peter 3:8, one day is with the Lord as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day; (6) 1 Timothy 1:17, the King eternal; (7) Isaiah 57:15, the high and lofty One that inhabiteth eternity. The Reformed-confessional doctrine (Westminster Confession II.1, God is eternal; the Reformed-scholastic doctrine of divine eternity) holds that God is eternal in the fullness of His being, without beginning, end, or succession of moments. The substantive theological implications: God's eternality grounds His immutability (the eternal God does not change), His faithfulness (the eternal God's promises endure), and the believer's security (the eternal God is an everlasting refuge, Deuteronomy 33:27, the eternal God is thy refuge, and underneath are the everlasting arms). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive doctrine of divine eternality against the process-theology denial (which makes God temporal and developing) and the rationalist reduction (which treats eternity as mere endless time); God transcends time, inhabits eternity, and is the unchanging, everlasting, faithful refuge of His people.
webster_summary: The divine attribute by which God is without beginning or end, transcending time, existing in the fullness of His being; Psalm 90:2 (from everlasting to everlasting, thou art God); Exodus 3:14 (I AM THAT I AM); Revelation 1:8; grounds His immutability, faithfulness, and the believer's everlasting security.

Held against process-theology (temporal, developing God) and the rationalist reduction (eternity as mere endless time).

corruption_paragraphs: The eternality of God is held against two opposing errors. Process theology (and open theism in some forms) makes God temporal and developing, subject to the succession of moments, learning and changing as history unfolds; this contradicts the biblical doctrine of God who inhabits eternity (Isaiah 57:15) and is the same from everlasting to everlasting (Psalm 90:2). The rationalist reduction treats divine eternity as mere endless time (God as a being who has existed for infinite time and will continue forever), missing the deeper truth that God transcends time itself, existing in the fullness of His being above the temporal succession. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive Reformed-confessional doctrine: God is eternal, without beginning, end, or succession; He transcends time and inhabits eternity; His eternality grounds His immutability (the eternal God does not change), His faithfulness (the eternal God's promises endure across all generations), and the believer's everlasting security (the eternal God is the refuge underneath whom are the everlasting arms, Deuteronomy 33:27). The eternality of God is not a cold abstraction but a substantive comfort: the believer's God is the everlasting God, the same yesterday, today, and forever, whose eternal purposes cannot fail and whose eternal arms cannot weaken.

etymology: The divine attribute by which God is without limit or boundary in His being and perfections. God is infinite in His essence, His knowledge, His power, His presence, and all His attributes. Grounded in 1 Kings 8:27 (the heaven of heavens cannot contain thee), Psalm 147:5 (his understanding is infinite), and Job 11:7-9.
biblical_def: The divine attribute by which God is without limit or boundary in His being and perfections. God's infinity means that He is unbounded, unlimited, and immeasurable in His essence and in all His attributes — infinite in His being (He is not contained or circumscribed), infinite in His knowledge (His understanding is without limit), infinite in His power (nothing is too hard for Him), infinite in His presence (He fills heaven and earth), infinite in His holiness, goodness, wisdom, and every perfection. The biblical foundation: (1) 1 Kings 8:27, Solomon's confession at the temple dedication, But will God indeed dwell on the earth? behold, the heaven and heaven of heavens cannot contain thee; how much less this house that I have builded?; (2) Psalm 147:5, Great is our Lord, and of great power: his understanding is infinite; (3) Job 11:7-9, Canst thou by searching find out God? canst thou find out the Almighty unto perfection? It is as high as heaven; what canst thou do? deeper than hell; what canst thou know? The measure thereof is longer than the earth, and broader than the sea; (4) Psalm 145:3, Great is the LORD, and greatly to be praised; and his greatness is unsearchable; (5) Jeremiah 23:24, Do not I fill heaven and earth? saith the LORD. The Reformed-confessional doctrine (Westminster Confession II.1, God is infinite in being and perfection) holds that God is unlimited and immeasurable in His essence and all His attributes. The substantive theological implications: God's infinity means He cannot be contained, comprehended, or measured by the finite creature; it grounds His incomprehensibility (the finite cannot fully grasp the infinite); it humbles the creature before the immeasurable greatness of God; and it assures the believer of the inexhaustible sufficiency of his infinite God. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive doctrine of divine infinity against the finite-god conceptions (process theology, open theism, and the various reductions of God to a bounded being) and the pantheistic confusion (which dissolves the infinite God into the infinite universe); God is infinite in being and perfection, unbounded, immeasurable, and inexhaustible — the infinite God whom the heaven of heavens cannot contain.

etymology: The doctrine that God, being infinite, cannot be fully comprehended (exhaustively known) by the finite creature, though He can be truly known as He reveals Himself. Grounded in the unsearchableness of God (Romans 11:33-34; Job 11:7; Isaiah 40:28; Psalm 145:3). Distinguished from agnosticism (which denies that God can be truly known at all).
biblical_def: The doctrine that God, being infinite, cannot be fully comprehended (exhaustively known) by the finite creature, though He can be truly known as He reveals Himself. The doctrine holds two truths in balance. (1) God cannot be exhaustively comprehended: the finite creature cannot fully grasp the infinite God; God's ways and being exceed the creature's comprehension. O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! how unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out! For who hath known the mind of the Lord? (Romans 11:33-34); Canst thou by searching find out God? canst thou find out the Almighty unto perfection? (Job 11:7); there is no searching of his understanding (Isaiah 40:28); his greatness is unsearchable (Psalm 145:3). (2) God can be truly (though not exhaustively) known: God has revealed Himself truly in His works, His Word, and supremely in His Son, so that the creature can have true (though not comprehensive) knowledge of God. This is life eternal, that they might know thee the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent (John 17:3); the knowledge of God is the goal of redemption (Jeremiah 31:34; Hebrews 8:11). The Reformed-confessional doctrine holds the substantive balance: God is incomprehensible (not exhaustively knowable by the finite creature) but truly knowable (genuinely revealed and apprehensible as He has made Himself known). The substantive theological implications: the incomprehensibility of God humbles the creature, guards against rationalist presumption (the attempt to comprehend God by autonomous reason), and grounds the necessity of revelation (we know God only as He reveals Himself); while the true knowability of God assures the believer that his knowledge of God, though not comprehensive, is genuine and saving. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive doctrine against both rationalism (which presumes to comprehend God exhaustively by reason) and agnosticism / mysticism (which denies that God can be truly known at all). God is incomprehensible yet truly knowable: the creature cannot fully comprehend the infinite God, but can truly know Him as He has revealed Himself in His Word and in His Son.

corruption_paragraphs: The incomprehensibility of God is held against two opposing errors. Rationalism presumes to comprehend God exhaustively by autonomous reason, subjecting God to the categories and judgments of the finite human mind; this contradicts the biblical doctrine that God's judgments are unsearchable and His ways past finding out (Romans 11:33-34), that no one has known the mind of the Lord or been His counselor (Romans 11:34; Isaiah 40:13-14). Agnosticism and certain forms of mysticism deny that God can be truly known at all, treating God as utterly unknowable, beyond all true predication (the radical apophaticism that says we can only know what God is not); this contradicts the biblical doctrine that God has revealed Himself truly and that knowing Him is eternal life (John 17:3). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive Reformed-confessional balance: God is incomprehensible (the finite creature cannot exhaustively comprehend the infinite God) yet truly knowable (God has revealed Himself genuinely in His works, His Word, and supremely in His Son, so that the creature can have true and saving knowledge of God). Deuteronomy 29:29 holds the balance perfectly: the secret things belong to the LORD (the incomprehensible depths beyond the creature's grasp), but the revealed things belong to us and to our children forever (the true knowledge God has graciously given). The believer adores the incomprehensible greatness of God while resting in the true knowledge of Him that God has revealed; he does not presume to comprehend the infinite God by reason, nor despair of knowing Him truly, but receives with humility and gratitude the true knowledge of God that the incomprehensible God has graciously revealed.

etymology: The divine attribute by which God is spirit — an immaterial, non-corporeal being, without body, parts, or physical extension. Grounded in Christ's words to the Samaritan woman (John 4:24, God is a Spirit) and the second-commandment prohibition of images. Westminster Confession II.1 (God is a most pure spirit... without body, parts, or passions).
biblical_def: The divine attribute by which God is spirit — an immaterial, non-corporeal being, without body, parts, or physical extension. The foundational text is the Lord Jesus's declaration to the Samaritan woman: God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth (John 4:24). God's spirituality means He has no physical body and is not composed of material parts; He is invisible (1 Timothy 1:17, the King eternal, immortal, invisible), not localized in space as bodies are, and not perceptible by the physical senses. The Westminster Confession (II.1) describes God as a most pure spirit, invisible, without body, parts, or passions. The biblical anthropomorphisms (references to God's hand, arm, eyes, face, etc.) are figures of speech accommodating divine truth to human understanding, not literal descriptions of a divine body; God is spirit. The second-commandment prohibition of images (Exodus 20:4-6) is grounded in God's spirituality: because God is spirit, He cannot and must not be represented by any material image; every attempt to make a visible image of the invisible God falsifies His spiritual nature and constitutes idolatry. The incarnation is the unique exception that proves the rule: in the incarnation, the eternal Son (who as God is spirit) took to Himself a true human body and nature, becoming visible and tangible (1 John 1:1-3); but this does not make the divine nature corporeal; the divine nature remains spirit, and the human nature of Christ is the visible, tangible humanity He assumed. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive doctrine of God's spirituality against the anthropomorphite error (which attributes a literal body to God), the idolatrous image-making (which the second commandment forbids), and the materialist denial (which reduces all reality to matter). God is spirit; He must be worshiped in spirit and in truth; He cannot be represented by any material image; and the worship that pleases Him is spiritual worship grounded in truth, not the image-worship and sensory religion that violates His spiritual nature.

corruption_paragraphs: The spirituality of God is held against several errors. The anthropomorphite error attributes a literal physical body to God, reading the biblical anthropomorphisms (God's hand, arm, eyes, face) as literal descriptions of a divine body; this contradicts the explicit teaching that God is spirit (John 4:24) and invisible (1 Timothy 1:17). The idolatrous image-making attempts to represent God by material images; this is forbidden by the second commandment precisely because God is spirit and cannot be truly represented by any material likeness (every image of God falsifies His spiritual nature and constitutes idolatry). The materialist denial reduces all reality to matter, denying the existence of spirit altogether. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive doctrine: God is spirit — immaterial, non-corporeal, invisible, without body or parts; He must be worshiped in spirit and in truth (John 4:24); He cannot and must not be represented by any material image (the second-commandment ground); the worship that pleases Him is spiritual worship grounded in His revealed truth, not image-worship and sensory religion. The substantive implication for worship is significant: the regulative principle of worship, the rejection of images in worship, and the centrality of the Word (the means by which the invisible spiritual God reveals Himself) all flow from the spirituality of God. The believer worships the invisible, spiritual God in spirit and in truth, through the Word and the appointed spiritual means, not through images and sensory religion that violate God's spiritual nature.

etymology: The divine attribute by which God in His essence is invisible — not perceptible by physical sight. Grounded in 1 Timothy 1:17 (invisible), 1 Timothy 6:16 (whom no man hath seen, nor can see), John 1:18 (no man hath seen God at any time), and Colossians 1:15 (the invisible God). Closely related to the spirituality of God.
biblical_def: The divine attribute by which God in His essence is invisible — not perceptible by physical sight. Closely related to the spirituality of God (because God is spirit, He is invisible). The biblical foundation: (1) 1 Timothy 1:17, the King eternal, immortal, invisible, the only wise God; (2) 1 Timothy 6:16, Whom no man hath seen, nor can see; (3) John 1:18, No man hath seen God at any time; the only begotten Son, which is in the bosom of the Father, he hath declared him; (4) Colossians 1:15, Christ is the image of the invisible God; (5) Exodus 33:20, the LORD's words to Moses, Thou canst not see my face: for there shall no man see me, and live; (6) John 4:24 with John 6:46, Not that any man hath seen the Father, save he which is of God, he hath seen the Father. The doctrine holds that God in His essence cannot be seen by the physical eye; the theophanies of the OT (the visible manifestations of God — the burning bush, the glory-cloud, the appearances to the patriarchs) were accommodated visible manifestations of God's presence and glory, not the seeing of God's invisible essence; and the supreme revelation of the invisible God is the Lord Jesus Christ, who as the image of the invisible God (Colossians 1:15) and the only-begotten Son in the bosom of the Father has declared (made known) the invisible God (John 1:18). The eschatological hope includes the beatific vision — the seeing of God (Matthew 5:8, the pure in heart... shall see God; 1 John 3:2, we shall see him as he is; Revelation 22:4, they shall see his face) — understood by the Reformed tradition as the glorified saints' immediate and blessed knowledge-and-sight of God in a manner exceeding present comprehension, supremely in the face of Christ. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive doctrine of God's invisibility against the idolatrous image-making (the attempt to make visible the invisible God), and grounds in it the central role of the Word (the invisible God reveals Himself by His Word, heard rather than seen) and the supreme revelation of God in Christ (the image of the invisible God who declares the Father).

The believer worships the invisible God through the Word and in Christ, refusing the idolatrous image-making that would make visible the invisible God, and awaits the beatific vision when faith shall give way to sight.

etymology: The divine attribute by which God is zealous for His own glory and for the exclusive devotion of His covenant people, refusing to share His worship with idols. Grounded in the second commandment (Exodus 20:5, I the LORD thy God am a jealous God) and the divine name (Exodus 34:14, the LORD, whose name is Jealous). Distinguished from sinful human jealousy/envy.
biblical_def: The divine attribute by which God is zealous for His own glory and for the exclusive devotion of His covenant people, refusing to share His worship with idols or rivals. Divine jealousy is a holy and righteous attribute, sharply distinguished from the sinful human passions of jealousy and envy. The biblical foundation: (1) the second commandment, Thou shalt not bow down thyself to them, nor serve them: for I the LORD thy God am a jealous God (Exodus 20:5; Deuteronomy 5:9); (2) the divine name, For thou shalt worship no other god: for the LORD, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God (Exodus 34:14); (3) the warnings against provoking God to jealousy by idolatry (Deuteronomy 32:16, 21, They provoked him to jealousy with strange gods; Psalm 78:58; 1 Corinthians 10:22, Do we provoke the Lord to jealousy? are we stronger than he?); (4) the marital imagery of God's jealous love for His covenant people (the prophets' portrayal of Israel's idolatry as spiritual adultery against her jealous husband the LORD, Hosea, Ezekiel 16, 23; Jeremiah 3). God's jealousy is the righteous zeal of His holy love: as a faithful husband is rightly jealous for the exclusive devotion of his wife (and would be deficient in love if he were indifferent to her adultery), so the LORD is rightly jealous for the exclusive worship and devotion of His covenant people, and is rightly provoked to jealousy by their idolatry (spiritual adultery). Divine jealousy is therefore the holy obverse of divine love: precisely because God loves His people with a holy covenant love, He is jealous for their exclusive devotion and zealous against the idols that would steal their worship. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive doctrine of divine jealousy against the sentimental reduction (which treats God as indifferently tolerant, sharing His worship with all rivals) and the misunderstanding that confuses holy divine jealousy with sinful human envy. God is jealous for His glory and for the exclusive devotion of His people; idolatry provokes His righteous jealousy; and the believer is called to the exclusive, whole-hearted devotion that the jealous love of God both demands and deserves.

A holy and righteous attribute, distinguished from sinful human jealousy/envy. Foundation: the second commandment (Exodus 20:5, I the LORD thy God am a jealous God); the divine name (Exodus 34:14, the LORD, whose name is Jealous); the warnings against provoking God to jealousy by idolatry (Deuteronomy 32:16, 21; 1 Corinthians 10:22); the marital imagery of God's jealous covenant love (Hosea; Ezekiel 16). The holy obverse of divine love: because God loves His people with holy covenant love, He is jealous for their exclusive devotion. Held against the sentimental reduction (indifferent tolerance) and the confusion with sinful envy.

corruption_summary: The jealousy of God is the holy obverse of His covenant love, distinguished from sinful human envy; the corruptions are the sentimental reduction (treating God as indifferently tolerant) and the confusion of holy divine jealousy with sinful human jealousy.
corruption_paragraphs: The jealousy of God is held against two errors. The sentimental reduction treats God as indifferently tolerant, a benign deity content to share His worship with all rivals, untroubled by the idolatry of His people; this contradicts the substantive biblical witness that the LORD is a jealous God (Exodus 20:5; 34:14; Deuteronomy 4:24, a consuming fire, even a jealous God) who is provoked to righteous jealousy by idolatry. The confusion of holy divine jealousy with sinful human jealousy treats divine jealousy as a defect, a petty insecurity unworthy of God; this fails to distinguish the holy righteous jealousy of God (the zeal of His holy love for the exclusive devotion of His people) from the sinful human passions of envy and possessive insecurity. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive doctrine: divine jealousy is a holy and righteous attribute, the obverse of divine love. As a faithful husband is rightly jealous for the exclusive faithfulness of his wife (and would be deficient in love if he were indifferent to her adultery), so the LORD is rightly jealous for the exclusive worship and devotion of His covenant people, and is rightly provoked to jealousy by their idolatry (which the prophets portray as spiritual adultery). Divine jealousy is not a defect but a perfection: precisely because God loves His people with a holy covenant love, He is jealous for their exclusive devotion and zealous against the idols that would steal their worship. The believer is called to the exclusive, whole-hearted devotion that the jealous love of God both demands and deserves, fleeing idolatry and giving God the undivided worship that is His due.

etymology: The divine attribute by which God is in Himself the perfect and the source of all good, and is benevolent, kind, and bountiful toward His creatures. Grounded in the divine self-revelation (Exodus 33:19, I will make all my goodness pass before thee), the creation refrain, and the psalms (Psalm 100:5, the LORD is good; Psalm 145:9, the LORD is good to all).
biblical_def: The divine attribute by which God is in Himself the perfect good and the source of all good, and is benevolent, kind, generous, and bountiful toward His creatures. The goodness of God has both an absolute dimension (God is good in Himself, the perfect and the standard of all goodness) and a relative dimension (God is good toward His creatures, doing them good). The biblical foundation: (1) God is good in Himself — none is good, save one, that is, God (Mark 10:18; Luke 18:19); God is the standard and source of all goodness (every good gift comes from Him, James 1:17). (2) God revealed His goodness to Moses — I will make all my goodness pass before thee (Exodus 33:19), the goodness being then defined in the proclamation of the divine name (Exodus 34:6-7, merciful, gracious, longsuffering, abundant in goodness and truth). (3) The psalms repeatedly celebrate God's goodness — O give thanks unto the LORD; for he is good: for his mercy endureth for ever (Psalm 107:1; 118:1; 136:1); For the LORD is good; his mercy is everlasting (Psalm 100:5); The LORD is good to all: and his tender mercies are over all his works (Psalm 145:9); O taste and see that the LORD is good (Psalm 34:8). The various aspects of God's goodness include His benevolence (His kind disposition toward His creatures), His grace (His goodness toward the undeserving), His mercy (His goodness toward the miserable), His longsuffering (His goodness toward the guilty in withholding deserved judgment), and His common grace (His goodness toward all creatures, the just and the unjust, Matthew 5:45). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive doctrine of God's goodness against the dualistic and gnostic conceptions (which attribute evil to God or to a co-equal evil principle) and the sentimental reduction (which reduces God's goodness to indulgent permissiveness, divorced from His holiness and justice). God is good — perfectly good in Himself, the source and standard of all good, and benevolent, gracious, merciful, and bountiful toward His creatures — and His goodness is held together with His holiness and justice, so that the same good God is also the holy God who will by no means clear the guilty (Exodus 34:7). The goodness of God is the substantive ground of the believer's gratitude, trust, and worship.

corruption_paragraphs: The goodness of God is held against two errors. The dualistic and gnostic conceptions attribute evil to God or posit a co-equal evil principle alongside the good God; this contradicts the biblical doctrine that God is good (Mark 10:18), the source of every good gift (James 1:17), good to all (Psalm 145:9). The sentimental reduction reduces God's goodness to indulgent permissiveness — a benign deity whose goodness consists in tolerating all things and judging nothing, divorced from His holiness and justice; this contradicts the biblical revelation in which the same proclamation that declares God merciful, gracious, and abundant in goodness also declares that He will by no means clear the guilty (Exodus 34:6-7). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive doctrine: God is good — perfectly good in Himself, the source and standard of all good, benevolent, gracious, merciful, longsuffering, and bountiful toward His creatures — and His goodness is held together with His holiness and justice. The goodness of God is not opposed to His justice but integrated with it: His goodness includes His grace toward the undeserving and His mercy toward the miserable, but also His holy opposition to evil and His just judgment of sin. The cross is the supreme display of God's goodness held together with His justice: in the substitutionary atonement, God's goodness (His gracious salvation of sinners) and His justice (His full satisfaction of the penalty for sin) meet without compromise. The goodness of God is the substantive ground of the believer's gratitude, trust, and worship: O give thanks unto the LORD; for he is good (Psalm 107:1).

etymology: The divine attribute (also called longsuffering or forbearance) by which God patiently bears with sinners, withholding deserved judgment and giving space for repentance. Grounded in the divine self-revelation (Exodus 34:6, longsuffering), 2 Peter 3:9 (longsuffering... not willing that any should perish), and Romans 2:4 (the riches of his goodness and forbearance and longsuffering).
biblical_def: The divine attribute (also called longsuffering or forbearance) by which God patiently bears with sinners, withholding deserved judgment and giving space for repentance. God's patience is an aspect of His goodness directed toward the guilty: as mercy is His goodness toward the miserable and grace is His goodness toward the undeserving, so patience (longsuffering) is His goodness toward the guilty, expressed in His withholding of the judgment they deserve and His granting of time and opportunity for repentance. The biblical foundation: (1) the divine self-revelation, The LORD, The LORD God, merciful and gracious, longsuffering, and abundant in goodness and truth (Exodus 34:6); (2) Romans 2:4, Or despisest thou the riches of his goodness and forbearance and longsuffering; not knowing that the goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance?; (3) 2 Peter 3:9, The Lord is not slack concerning his promise, as some men count slackness; but is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance; (4) 1 Peter 3:20, the longsuffering of God waiting in the days of Noah; (5) Romans 9:22, God, willing to shew his wrath, and to make his power known, endured with much longsuffering the vessels of wrath fitted to destruction. God's patience is displayed throughout redemptive history: His longsuffering with the antediluvian world (1 Peter 3:20), with Israel's repeated rebellions (Nehemiah 9:17, 30-31, thou art a God ready to pardon... slow to anger, and of great kindness), and with sinners in every age. The patience of God is not indifference to sin or weakness in judgment; it is the deliberate withholding of deserved judgment to give space for repentance, and it has limits — the patience of God, despised and presumed upon, gives way to judgment when the appointed time comes (Genesis 6:3; Romans 2:5, the treasuring up of wrath against the day of wrath). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive doctrine of God's patience against the presumption that abuses it (treating God's delay of judgment as license for continued sin, 2 Peter 3:3-9; Ecclesiastes 8:11) and the impatience that despairs of it (failing to recognize the longsuffering goodness of God that leads to repentance, Romans 2:4). God is patient — longsuffering, forbearing, slow to anger — bearing with sinners and giving space for repentance; His patience is a substantive expression of His goodness, leading sinners to repentance, and is not to be presumed upon or despised.

corruption_paragraphs: The patience of God is held against two errors. The presumption that abuses God's patience treats His delay of judgment as license for continued sin: because sentence against an evil work is not executed speedily, therefore the heart of the sons of men is fully set in them to do evil (Ecclesiastes 8:11); the scoffers presume upon God's longsuffering, mocking the delay of judgment (2 Peter 3:3-4). This contradicts the biblical teaching that God's patience is meant to lead to repentance (Romans 2:4), not to embolden sin, and that the abuse of God's patience treasures up wrath against the day of wrath (Romans 2:5). The impatience that despairs of God's patience fails to recognize the longsuffering goodness of God, supposing that God's delay of judgment means He does not see or care; this contradicts the biblical teaching that God's apparent slowness is His longsuffering, not willing that any should perish (2 Peter 3:9). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive doctrine: God is patient — longsuffering, forbearing, slow to anger — bearing with sinners and giving space for repentance; His patience is a substantive expression of His goodness, designed to lead sinners to repentance (Romans 2:4); but His patience is not indifference to sin nor weakness in judgment, and it has limits — the patience of God, despised and presumed upon, gives way to judgment when the appointed time comes (Genesis 6:3; the flood; the patience that waited in Noah's day eventually gave way to the deluge). The believer responds to God's patience with repentance and gratitude, neither presuming upon it as license for sin nor despairing of it in the face of delayed judgment, but recognizing the longsuffering goodness of God that leads to repentance and extends the day of salvation.

etymology: The divine attribute by which God is true — the true God (as opposed to false gods), truthful in all His words (He cannot lie), and faithful to all His promises. Grounded in the divine self-description (Numbers 23:19, God is not a man, that he should lie; Titus 1:2, God, that cannot lie; John 17:17, thy word is truth).
biblical_def: The divine attribute by which God is true. Divine veracity (truthfulness) has three integrated dimensions. (1) God is the true God (as opposed to the false gods / idols): He is the real, genuine, only true God (John 17:3, the only true God; 1 Thessalonians 1:9, turning from idols to serve the living and true God; Jeremiah 10:10, the LORD is the true God). (2) God is truthful — He speaks only truth and cannot lie: God is not a man, that he should lie (Numbers 23:19); in hope of eternal life, which God, that cannot lie, promised (Titus 1:2); it was impossible for God to lie (Hebrews 6:18); let God be true, but every man a liar (Romans 3:4). (3) God is faithful — He keeps all His promises and is reliable in all His dealings: God is faithful (1 Corinthians 1:9; 10:13); he abideth faithful: he cannot deny himself (2 Timothy 2:13); faithful is he that calleth you, who also will do it (1 Thessalonians 5:24); great is thy faithfulness (Lamentations 3:23). The veracity of God grounds the trustworthiness of His Word (John 17:17, thy word is truth; Psalm 119:160, thy word is true from the beginning) and the reliability of His promises (the believer can stake everything on God's promises because the God who made them cannot lie and is faithful to fulfill them). The substantive theological implications: divine veracity grounds the authority and reliability of Scripture (the Word of the God who cannot lie is itself true and reliable, the foundation of biblical inerrancy); it grounds the assurance of faith (the believer rests on the promises of the God who cannot lie); and it grounds the integrity of the Christian life (the people of the true and truthful God are called to truthfulness, putting away lying, Ephesians 4:25). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive doctrine of God's veracity against the relativism that denies objective truth, the conceptions of a deceptive or arbitrary deity, and the doubt that questions the reliability of God's Word and promises. God is true — the only true God, truthful in all His words (He cannot lie), and faithful to all His promises — and His veracity is the substantive ground of the reliability of His Word, the assurance of faith, and the integrity of the Christian life.

corruption_paragraphs: The veracity of God is held against several errors. Relativism denies objective truth altogether, treating all truth-claims as relative human constructions; this contradicts the biblical doctrine that God is true, that His Word is truth (John 17:17), and that truth is grounded in the true and truthful God. The conceptions of a deceptive or arbitrary deity (the nominalist conception of a God who could declare anything true or good by arbitrary will, the deceiver-god of certain skeptical thought-experiments) contradict the biblical doctrine that God cannot lie (Titus 1:2; Hebrews 6:18) and is faithful and unchanging in His truthfulness. The doubt that questions the reliability of God's Word and promises (the practical unbelief that fails to rest on God's promises) contradicts the biblical assurance that the God who promised cannot lie and is faithful to fulfill (Numbers 23:19; 2 Timothy 2:13). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive doctrine: God is true — the only true God (as opposed to the false gods), truthful in all His words (He cannot lie), and faithful to all His promises. The veracity of God is the substantive ground of three great realities: the authority and reliability of Scripture (the Word of the God who cannot lie is itself true and inerrant, the foundation of the doctrine of Scripture); the assurance of faith (the believer can stake everything on God's promises because the God who made them cannot lie and is faithful to fulfill them); and the integrity of the Christian life (the people of the true and truthful God are called to truthfulness, putting away lying, speaking truth, Ephesians 4:25). The believer rests on the veracity of God: His Word is true, His promises are sure, and His faithfulness is great (Lamentations 3:23).

etymology: The divine attribute by which God exercises supreme, absolute, and universal rule over all His creation, governing all things according to the counsel of His own will. Grounded in the divine kingship and dominion (Psalm 103:19, his kingdom ruleth over all; Daniel 4:35; Ephesians 1:11, who worketh all things after the counsel of his own will). Central to Reformed theology.
biblical_def: The divine attribute by which God exercises supreme, absolute, and universal rule over all His creation, governing all things according to the counsel of His own will. The sovereignty of God is the substantive heart of Reformed theology, the truth that God is King over all, working all things according to His eternal purpose. The biblical foundation: (1) God's universal kingship and dominion — The LORD hath prepared his throne in the heavens; and his kingdom ruleth over all (Psalm 103:19); he doeth according to his will in the army of heaven, and among the inhabitants of the earth: and none can stay his hand, or say unto him, What doest thou? (Daniel 4:35); (2) God works all things according to His will — who worketh all things after the counsel of his own will (Ephesians 1:11); The LORD hath made all things for himself (Proverbs 16:4); Our God is in the heavens: he hath done whatsoever he hath pleased (Psalm 115:3); (3) God's sovereignty in creation (Genesis 1; all things made by His word), providence (Matthew 10:29-30, not a sparrow falls without the Father; Colossians 1:17, by Him all things consist), and salvation (Romans 9, the sovereignty of God in election and reprobation; Ephesians 1:4-11, election according to the good pleasure of His will); (4) God's sovereignty over the nations, kings, and history (Daniel 2:21, he removeth kings, and setteth up kings; Daniel 4:17, the most High ruleth in the kingdom of men; Proverbs 21:1, the king's heart is in the hand of the LORD); (5) God's sovereignty even over evil, which He ordains and overrules for His good purposes without being the author of sin (Genesis 50:20, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good; Acts 2:23, Christ delivered by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God yet by wicked hands crucified; Acts 4:27-28). The Reformed-confessional doctrine (Westminster Confession III on God's eternal decree; V on providence) holds that God from all eternity did freely and unchangeably ordain whatsoever comes to pass, yet so as neither to be the author of sin nor to do violence to the will of the creatures. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive doctrine of God's sovereignty as the heart of Reformed theology, against the open-theist and process-theology denials (which limit God's sovereignty), the deistic conception (which removes God's active governance), and the man-centered theologies (which subordinate God's sovereignty to human autonomy). God is sovereign — supreme, absolute, and universal in His rule, working all things according to the counsel of His own will — and His sovereignty is the substantive ground of the believer's confidence, comfort, and worship: nothing is outside God's control, all things work together for good to them that love God (Romans 8:28), and the King who reigns over all is the believer's Father.

corruption_paragraphs: The sovereignty of God is the substantive heart of Reformed theology, held against several errors. Open theism and process theology limit God's sovereignty, denying that God ordains and controls all things (open theism holds that God does not know or determine the free future actions of creatures; process theology makes God a developing participant in a process He does not control); this contradicts the biblical doctrine that God works all things after the counsel of His own will (Ephesians 1:11) and that none can stay His hand (Daniel 4:35). The deistic conception removes God's active governance, treating God as a distant creator who set the world in motion and does not actively rule it; this contradicts the biblical doctrine of God's active providence (Matthew 10:29-30; Colossians 1:17). The man-centered theologies (Arminianism in its various forms; the broader free-will theologies) subordinate God's sovereignty to human autonomy, making God's purposes contingent on the autonomous choices of the creature; this contradicts the biblical doctrine of God's sovereign election and His working of all things according to His will. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive Reformed-confessional doctrine: God is sovereign — supreme, absolute, and universal in His rule, working all things according to the counsel of His own will; His sovereignty extends over creation, providence, salvation, the nations and kings, and even over evil (which He ordains and overrules for His good purposes without being the author of sin, the great mystery held in Genesis 50:20 and Acts 2:23). The Westminster Confession holds the substantive balance (III.1): God from all eternity did freely and unchangeably ordain whatsoever comes to pass, yet so as neither to be the author of sin, nor is violence offered to the will of the creatures. The sovereignty of God is the substantive ground of the believer's confidence, comfort, and worship: nothing is outside God's control; all things work together for good to them that love God (Romans 8:28); the King who reigns supreme over all is the believer's loving Father, and His sovereign purposes cannot fail.
